claims.claim: Open-weight language models that often answer negated questions wrongly ('An animal that is not an amphibian is a ...' answered with 'frog') do internally register the negation, and their wrong answers come from attention in the later layers pushing the answer that fits the un-negated phrase. Supported only if, on a controlled set of matched positive and negated prompts, models from at least five families are above 90% accurate on positive prompts but no better than about 60% on negated ones, while for more than 90% of matched pairs the negation still moves the model's preference toward the negated answer; and if stopping attention from reading other tokens from some middle-to-late layer onward, leaving everything else intact, raises negated-prompt accuracy by at least 7 points in every model, more than simply reading the answer off at that layer, with the best starting layer past the middle of the network.
claims.decision_rule: Positive acc >90%, negative acc <=~60%, sensitivity >90% in >=5 families; cumulative late-layer attention ablation raises negative acc >=7 pts in every model and beats logit lens at that layer, best layer > 0.5L.

claims.claim: Language models process a negated phrase 'not Y' mainly by building and passing forward a representation of what 'not Y' refers to (for 'not a gas', something like 'solid'), and only secondarily by suppressing Y itself. Supported only if, in the models analysed: negation can be linearly decoded at the position of Y from early layers; a band of middle-layer attention modules is causally necessary for correct negated answers, shown both by disabling them and by patching their outputs in from the positive prompt; projecting those modules' outputs onto the vocabulary shows tokens related to 'not Y' among the top promoted tokens for more than 80% of examples, peaking at the same layers, while tokens related to Y appear among the most suppressed for clearly fewer examples; and downstream MLP features can be found that promote concrete instances of the negated concept.
claims.decision_rule: Negation linearly decodable early at Y; mid-layer attention causally necessary (sink + path patching); 'not Y' promoted in >80% of examples vs Y suppressed in a smaller share, same peak layer; SAE latents promoting negated concept.

experiments.text: Build a controlled negation dataset and its scores. Setup: prompts of the form 'X that is not Y is Z', each with a positive twin differing only by the negation word (not, no, cannot), and single-token answers correct for each (e.g. frog / mammal); 162 questions in 4 templates, 648 entries, grouped by subject category. Read logits at the last prompt position; positive and negative accuracy are the shares of prompts whose correct answer out-logits the other; sensitivity is the share of pairs where the logit difference (negated answer minus positive answer) is larger on the negated prompt than on the positive one.

Show the gap between output accuracy and internal sensitivity. Setup: score six open-weight models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Gemma-2, Mistral-7B-v0.1, OLMo-2) on the dataset. Result: positive accuracy 91.8-96.5%, negative accuracy only 45.2-57.6% (Mistral 45.2, Gemma 49.7, Llama 50.5), yet sensitivity 95.1-97.8%: the negation almost always moves preference in the right direction without flipping the answer. An appendix test checks that sensitivity is not an artefact of randomness.

Switch off late attention and see whether negated answers recover. Setup: 'attention sinking' restricts a head so the current token may attend only to itself and the first token, removing information movement while keeping value and MLP computation on the current token; justify it as mild by showing that the last token already puts 63.9-79.5% of its attention on those two tokens. Apply it cumulatively from a chosen layer to the end and report the best layer; compare with reading the logit lens at that layer, which skips later layers entirely. Result: negative accuracy rises in all six models: Llama 50.5 to 67.8 (logit lens 53.6), Qwen2.5 57.6 to 65.4, Qwen3 55.7 to 64.2, Gemma-2 49.7 to 66.1, Mistral 45.2 to 65.9 (a 46% relative gain), OLMo-2 54.0 to 68.7, always more than the logit-lens shortcut, and the best layer is always past half the depth.

Check that the late attention being removed is not what makes positive prompts right. Setup: sweep the starting layer of cumulative attention sinking and plot positive and negative accuracy against it. Result: modules after the best negative-accuracy layer contribute only to positive accuracy, and by that layer positive accuracy is already close to its unablated value, so the shortcut modules are largely separate from those that answer positive prompts.

Trace when the shortcut appears in training. Setup: evaluate positive accuracy, negative accuracy and sensitivity on OLMo-2 pretraining checkpoints from about 1e3 to 1e6 steps. Result: negative accuracy first plunges early in training, then rises again and stabilises around chance, while sensitivity to negation is present from an early stage, consistent with an early-forming bias toward positive answers on negated prompts.

Test whether negation is carried to the position of the negated phrase. Setup: for each pair, take hidden states at the last token of Y at every layer in Llama-3.1-8B; with 10-fold cross-validation, reduce each layer to two principal components, fit linear discriminant analysis on positive versus negated labels, keep the best direction, project all layers onto it and report held-out decoding accuracy by layer. Result: positive and negated states separate along roughly one direction, and negation is decoded with near-perfect accuracy by layer 4.

Find which attention modules are causally needed for negation. Setup: on Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B with an expanded prompt set, (a) sink attention only at the last position in sliding windows of 1-5 layers, keeping attention patterns fixed elsewhere, and track negative accuracy against window centre; (b) path-patch attention outputs at the last position from the positive prompt into the negated prompt at sets of layers, holding attention patterns fixed and recomputing MLPs, and count how often a correct negated answer flips to the positive one. Result: sinking windows around layer 14 makes negative accuracy drop sharply, sinking around layer 17 improves it (the shortcut heads), and later layers barely matter; path patching identifies the same middle-layer modules in both models.

Read what the causal attention modules write. Setup: project the last-position attention outputs of layers 10-18 on negated prompts onto the vocabulary, take the top 10 promoted and bottom 10 suppressed tokens per layer, and ask an LLM annotator (gpt-oss-120b) whether each relates to 'not Y' or to Y; count examples with at least one match per layer. Result: for over 80% of examples some layer promotes tokens related to 'not Y' (gas to solid, in Asia to America, near the ocean to inland), and for over 30% some layer suppresses tokens related to Y (Europe suppressing europe, Europeans); both peak at layer 14, the causally important layer, with suppression clearly less frequent than construction.

Find the MLP features that turn the constructed representation into the answer. Setup: in Llama-3.1-8B, score each MLP's contribution to the (negated answer minus positive answer) unembedding direction, contrasting the negated prompt with its positive twin and with the attention-sunk negated prompt; intersect the top 10 of each to get critical MLPs (about layers 17-25); decompose them with pretrained sparse autoencoders, score latents the same way, and manually inspect top latents with the logit lens (about 20 samples, 50 latents each). Result: promoting latents found for 8 samples, 13 interpretable in total, which directly instantiate the negated concept (not gaseous at room temperature to metal, silver; not in Asia to England, London, USA; not open source to Windows, .exe); top suppressed tokens of these latents are mostly uninterpretable; for other samples latents were uninterpretable or reconstruction error dominated.
